metadata.section: Chapter 13: EXPANDING THE BASIC BREEDER'S EQUATION
metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: breeders, experimentalists, and natural selection all may use additional information in determining the fitness of individuals. For example, one may measure traits in one set of individuals and then use this information to predict the mean breeding value for a second set of related individuals that will be the actual parents of the next generation. One such setting is family selection, wherein one measures the values of a number of family members (for example, by growing seed from a family over a number of environments) and, based on their means, selects the exceptional families. Remnant seeds from these families (i.e., seeds whose phenotypes are not scored) are then used to form the next generation. The prediction of the selection response now involves predicting the breeding value of a family member given the mean of other family members. The breeder's equation is easily extended to these more complex settings, as we now demonstrate. The structure of the general selection problem is given by Figure 13.2.
